props.title: The Fortune Cookie
props.initialSlug: Shyster lawyer exploits cameraman's fake injury

sections.content: The Fortune Cookie marks a pivotal moment in Billy Wilder's career, reuniting Jack Lemmon and Walter Matthau in their first on-screen partnership. This cynical comedy about an unscrupulous lawyer who convinces his brother-in-law to fake an injury for insurance money perfectly bridges Wilder's earlier screwball works like Some Like It Hot (1959) with his later, darker comedies. Matthau's Oscar-winning performance as "Whiplash Willie" Gingrich established the sleazy-but-lovable persona he'd perfect throughout his career, while Lemmon continues the everyman tradition he mastered in The Apartment (1960).

sections.content: The film's cynical take on insurance fraud and ambulance-chasing lawyers feels remarkably prescient today. Wilder's trademark wit cuts deeper here than in his earlier comedies, setting the stage for similarly caustic legal comedies like ...And Justice for All (1979) and My Cousin Vinny (1992). The black-and-white cinematography by Joseph LaShelle creates a gritty, newspaper-like quality that enhances the film's satirical edge.

Beyond its comedy, The Fortune Cookie explores themes of moral compromise and redemption that would become increasingly central to American cinema in the late 1960s. The film's influence can be traced through later works like The Hospital (1971) and Network (1976), which similarly used dark humor to critique American institutions. sections.content: The chemistry between Lemmon and Matthau would go on to define both actors' careers, leading to numerous collaborations including Grumpy Old Men (1993) and Out to Sea (1997). Their partnership, which began with The Fortune Cookie, created a template for countless future buddy comedies, influencing everything from Midnight Run (1988) to Trading Places (1983).
